sections.figure_alt: A solid segment lies on a longer dashed line.
sections.body_md:
A set is convex when it contains the segment between any two of its points. If \(x\) and \(y\) are in the set and \(t\) is between 0 and 1, the combination \((1-t)x + ty\) has to be in the set. The endpoints themselves are the cases \(t = 0\) and \(t = 1\). Nothing in the definition requires the origin, a bound, or an open interior.

The sets that pass are the ones optimization uses constantly. Every ball of every norm is convex, open or closed. Every half-space is convex, open or closed. Every affine set is convex: subspaces, lines, and hyperplanes. An intersection of any family of convex sets is convex, so a set cut out by several linear inequalities is convex. A union is not safe. Two disks with a gap between them are each convex, and their union is not, because a bridge across the gap leaves both disks.

A finite convex combination stays in a convex set as well. Weights that are nonnegative and sum to 1, on any number of points of the set, produce another point of the set. The two-point definition is the one to check; the finite version follows from it.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\(C\) is convex when \(x, y \in C\) and \(t \in [0, 1]\) imply \((1-t)x + ty \in C\). For a closed half-space,
\[
a^T\bigl((1-t)x + ty\bigr) = (1-t)\, a^T x + t\, a^T y \le (1-t)b + tb = b.
\]
For a ball of a norm, the same combination satisfies the triangle inequality, so the ball is convex. If every set in a family is convex, the intersection is convex.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Consider the half-space \(x_1 + 3 x_2 \le 12\). The point \((6, 0)\) gives left-hand side 6. The point \((0, 4)\) gives 12. Both points belong. Their midpoint is \((3, 2)\), and
\[
3 + 3 \cdot 2 = 9.
\]
The left-hand side is 9, which is still at most 12. The same 9 is the average of 6 and 12, because the constraint is linear: the value at a midpoint is the midpoint of the values. A point such as \((6, 4)\) gives \(6 + 12 = 18\), which is outside. The segment from \((6, 0)\) to \((0, 4)\) never reaches that outside point.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: A union of convex sets need not be convex. The argument that each piece contains its own segments forgets segments that jump from one piece to the other. A circle, the boundary of a disk, is not convex: the chord cuts through the interior. Requiring the origin is a different property, and an affine line that misses the origin is still convex. An intersection preserves convexity even when infinitely many sets are involved. A quadratic constraint can destroy it. The disk \(x^2 + y^2 \le 1\) is convex, while the outside \(x^2 + y^2 \ge 1\) is not.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A polyhedron is an intersection of finitely many half-spaces, hence convex, and its extreme points are the vertices a simplex method uses. The domain of a convex function has to be a convex set, because the chord definition evaluates the function along segments. Over a convex feasible set, a local minimizer of a convex objective is global, and the proof moves along the segment from the local minimizer to any other feasible point.
